NEWS FROM THE BOARD NEWS FROM THE BOARD A monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners If you’ve ever heard of Drug Court, you likely know how this Ada County program changes lives and reunites families and loved ones. The facility where Drug Court participants attend classes, counseling and complete their urine analyses (UAs) is home to several other treatment courts including Veteran’s Court and Mental Health Court. They are all housed in the Ada County Treatment Services Center (ACTS) near Vista Avenue and I-84. On Friday January 31, 2025, the Ada County Board of Commissioners and Idaho’s Fourth Judicial District hosted a Community Open House at the facility on Elder Street in Boise. The Community Open House provided a rare look inside for visitors. We were honored to have distinguished guests on hand including Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, Garden City Mayor John Evans, members of the Idaho Supreme Court and judges of the Fourth Judicial District. A special thank you to everyone in trial court administration, treatment court staff and our judges. We are also grateful for the hundreds of treatment court participants who work hard to complete rigorous programs that allow them to reclaim their lives. Welcome to the monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners. We are happy to share information on significant news and events in Ada County. January 2025 Ryan Davidson Rod Beck Tom Dayley ADA COUNTY TREATMENT SERVICES CENTER (ACTS) COMMUNITY OPEN HOUSE Sandra Barrios, Ada County Trial Court Administrator

3 The Ada County Zoning Ordinance Amendment process began in 2020. This month, (January 2025) the final draft went before the Planning and Zoning Commission ahead of adoption. A few weeks before the hearing, we launched a website providing an overview of the zoning ordinance rewrite, which we also shared on Ada County’s social media platforms. Shortly after, some residents told us they were unaware of the project. This feedback surprised us, as the project has been ongoing for four years with outreach throughout. Early in the project, we conducted significant outreach, including a survey on the current code, which received almost 800 responses. We also held numerous meetings with stakeholder groups in 2020 and 2021, all documented on our website: https://adacounty.id.gov/developmentservices/ administration/zoning-ordinance-amendment/. These meetings were livestreamed on our social media for public viewing. In 2022, our staff completed the draft ordinance. We held several open houses and posted the draft and summaries of proposed changes online. Feedback was mostly positive, though some arrived at the open houses concerned that the rewrite would resemble the City of Boise’s, which was more extensive. They expressed relief that our proposal was more straightforward and simpler once they learned that our priorities were to clean up formatting, update graphics, and reorganize content to make the code easier for homeowners to navigate. The draft ordinance then underwent legal review for over a year. After some fine-tuning, it was prepared for adoption. During this time, we began receiving more applications for industrial solar farms, prompting us to address those regulations, which were minimal in the current code. This was incorporated into the zoning ordinance amendment, and the solar farm ordinance went through its own outreach, including a separate survey with over 300 responses. More information can be found here: https://adacounty.id.gov/developmentservices/ solar-farms-zoning-ordinance-amendment/. In Fall 2024, we received the final ordinance from legal, ready for application. We created a webpage summarizing the changes (which had not shifted much since the open houses, other than the addition of a new solar ordinance) and began preparing for the hearing. When we received feedback that some people were unaware of the project, we realized additional open houses were necessary to ensure the public had a chance to learn about the proposed changes and provide feedback. We also recognized that the summary on the webpage was too vague and are working on a more detailed document explaining the proposal. Brianna Bustos Communications and Outreach Coordinator, Ada County Development Services ADA COUNTY DEVELOPMENT SERVICES EXTENDS TIMELINE FOR PUBLIC INPUT ON ZONING ORDINANCE AMENDMENT ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT In addition to elected offices, Ada County government includes thirteen individual departments. Each department provides important services to our residents in Star, Eagle, Meridian, Boise, Garden City, Kuna, and Unincorporated Ada County. These services include law enforcement protection, emergency preparedness, election services, parks & waterways, indigent services, juvenile services, solid waste management, the Western Idaho Fair, Weed, Pest & Mosquito Abatement and more. 5 ADA COUNTY IDAHOADA COUNTY IDAHO Established in 1864 ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT ELECTED OFFICIALS: Front row L-R: Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley, Ada County Commission Chairman Rod W. Beck, Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson Back row: L-R: Ada County Prosecutor Jan Bennetts, Ada County Coroner Rich Riffle, Ada County Treasurer Elizabeth Mahn, Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, Ada County Assessor Rebecca Arnold, and Ada County Sheriff Matthew Clifford Working together in partnership on behalf of the citizens of Ada County to keep our communities safe, healthy, and economically robust. Our decisions are informed by a commitment to protecting the quality of life of all Ada County residents and visitors in a fiscally responsible manner. Ada County is the largest county in Idaho by population. Ada County’s projected population by 2030 will be more than 715,000 people. Ada County encompasses more than 1,000 square miles of high desert beauty, peppered with rolling foothills and a sparkling river that gently winds through both urban and rural landscapes. Ada County includes Idaho’s Capital City, Boise, and is home to five other distinct municipalities: Star, Eagle, Meridian, Garden City and Kuna. The county is known for its rich agricultural heritage and abundant open spaces for recreation. Ada County’s Barber Park, in southeast Boise, is the put-in location for the annual Boise River Float. Expo Idaho in Ada County is home to the annual Western Idaho Fair, one of the biggest and most popular events in Idaho each year. In 2026 Ada County will unveil a new destination park adjacent to Expo Idaho alongside the Boise River connecting to the Greenbelt. The 50+ acre Park at Expo Idaho will have playgrounds, sports fields, large nature areas, places for live entertainment and much more. While Ada County is the state’s rapidly growing commerce and industry hub, protecting the area’s unique agricultural heritage now and in the years to come remains paramount for leaders across the county. To learn more about how Ada County serves you, your business and your family please visit our website adacounty.id.gov

8 Ada County Commissioners are always honored to speak to local businesses and civic groups. Meeting with residents in settings like this helps residents understand upcoming projects and priorities in Ada County. Plus, the commissioners get to hear from you! COMMISSIONER TOM DAYLEY SPEAKS TO KUNA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE Thank you to the Kuna Chamber of Commerce for hosting Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley at their monthly luncheon on January 16th. Commissioner Dayley outlined plans for The Park at Expo Idaho (to be completed in 2026) and explained how the county distributes your property tax dollars to various taxing districts. Commissioner Dayley also explained how counties in Idaho are mandated to carry out certain functions under Idaho Law. Did you know for instance that every county in Idaho is required to have a jail? Another factoid attendees found interesting is the percentage of your property tax dollars that go to cities and schools. Would your civic group like a guest speaker who can explain how county government works and how it affects you directly. Let us know! Just email eduncan@adacounty.id.gov Thank you for being engaged and interested in the functions and priorities of county government in Idaho.

9 Thank you to Leadership Boise for inviting Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck to speak to a group of 150 January 15th. 9 The Ada County Coroner’s Office received over 1800 reports of death in 2024. The number of reported deaths is an ever-increasing number due largely to the growth of the area. These cases are investigated by highly trained professionals who conduct their investigations consistent with national and accreditation standards from both the International Association of Coroner’s and Medical Examiners and the National Association of Medical Examiners. Ada County Coroner’s Office is proud to be one of six agencies in the United States with this dual accreditation. The investigations completed by these professionals are vital in the determination of the cause and manner of death, which plays a critical role safeguarding the community, working independently, yet closely, with public health, law enforcement, and the Prosecutor’s Office. To honor this highly specialized work, the Ada County Commissioners signed a proclamation designating January 19 through 25 as Coroner and Medicolegal Death Investigation Professionals’ Week. This proclamation recognizes the comprehensive investigations conducted with the highest level of compassion, integrity, and respect by Ada County Coroner’s Office personnel. Rich Riffle, Ada County Coroner CORONER’S OFFICE PROCLAMATION L-R: Rich Riffle, Ada County Coroner; Steve Russell, Jr. Medicolegal Death Investigator III; Rod Beck, Ada County Commission Chairman; Ryan Davidson, Ada County Commissioner; Tom Dayley, Ada County Commissioner

1010 Do you know anyone who could qualify for property tax relief? Did you know that these programs exist? Homestead Exemption Available to those who own and occupy their home as their primary residence, and make application prior to December 31, to the Assessor’s Office to qualify for that specific tax year. Property Tax Deferral Program This program defers the taxes on the home and up to one acre of land for qualified applicants. The deferred taxes become a lien on the property and have to be repaid to the State of Idaho. The applicant must meet one of the requirements of the Property Tax Reduction Program and have a combined income of $60,170 or less for 2024. Veterans Property Tax Reduction Available to those that meet the following: • Applicant is recognized as 100% service-con- nected disabled or receive 100% compen- sation due to individual unemployability by the US Department of Veterans Affairs as of January 1, 2025 • Owned and lived in your primary residence before April 15, 2025 • Property must have a Homestead Exemption Property Tax Reduction Available to those who own and occupy their home as their primary residence by April 15, 2025 and meet one of the following qualifying statuses below: • Over the age of 65 • Widow(er) of any age (not remarried) • Legally blind (any age) • Disabled through Social Security, Railroad or VA • Former POW/Hostage • Fatherless or mother- less child under the age of 18 Income for this program cannot exceed $37,810 after deducting unreimbursed medical expenses and the property must have a Homestead Exemption in place. All of the listed programs, with the exception of the Homestead Exemption, must be applied for each year with the County Assessor’s Office. For more information, please contact the Ada County Assessor’s office 208-287-7200.
